items.reason: Neither named instance exists in the tree — sast.yml triggers only on push/pull_request/schedule and never checks out a PR head under a privileged trigger, and every ${{ }} in agent-review.yml is bound in an env: block and read back as a quoted shell variable, with the only literal occurrences of both patterns sitting in prose that explains why they are forbidden; both were already blocking via scripts/actions-pin.mjs P2/P5/P7, so the specific gap could not be closed by this change. What was genuinely open is the CLASS rather than the instance, and that is what I closed: P2 now forbids the whole privileged-trigger family (workflow_run, issue_comment, pull_request_review, pull_request_review_comment as well as pull_request_target), with a new unit test that fails both when a workflow declares one and when the policy's list of them is shortened. The remaining scan finding, SHA-pinning the 25 first-party action refs, needs network and stays open.

lessons: systedo-case encodes its workflow-security invariants as a blocking repo-local policy script (scripts/actions-pin.mjs, rules P1-P8, run in sast.yml's `workflow-policy` job and inside `npm run check:ci`) and documents each rule in SECURITY.md. Read that script and the workflows' own comments before treating a dangerous-workflow finding here as real: those files deliberately quote the exact patterns they forbid in prose, and a text-matching scanner hits the explanation rather than an occurrence. The repository already knows this about itself — test-unit/delivery-contract.test.mjs strips comment lines before asserting over the same YAML, for the same reason.

When a dangerous-workflow finding turns out to be a false positive in a repo this hardened, the useful move is not to re-argue the instance but to check whether the rule behind it names only the famous member of a class. Here P2 forbade `pull_request_target` alone; `workflow_run`, `issue_comment` and the two review triggers reach the same privileged context and were unenforced. Extending the enumeration is rung-correct (all five pass today, so the rule can be blocking) and cheap.

This repository's action-pinning gap is a decision plus one networked command, not a build: `npm run actions:pin` resolves every tag to a SHA AND writes STRICT = true / RATCHET.pinned back into scripts/actions-pin.mjs in the same pass. An offline agent can neither close it nor usefully prepare it, and must not flip STRICT by hand — that turns a blocking gate red on a tree nobody changed.

Ascent lanes in this worktree get no command execution at all (even `node script.mjs` is refused), so any edit to a script inside `check:ci` ships unverified and master ships on push. Keep such edits additive and obviously-correct — a new enumerated constant and a regex that mirrors an existing one — and pair them with a unit test that a human can run, rather than restructuring gate logic.
